answers.answer: SCOPe places d1vmga_ (MazG-like) and d1y6xa1 (HisE-like) in the same superfamily, which is a remote homology claim. Superfamily membership means the two domains are inferred to share common ancestry, based on structural similarity and a shared catalytic role. It does not mean close sequence similarity, and it does not establish that they belong to the same family or are orthologs. As I recall, both sit in the all-alpha class and share a nucleotide pyrophosphohydrolase-type fold, but I have not verified the exact SCOPe release fold and superfamily codes, so treat those as unconfirmed. The shared functional theme is pyrophosphate-releasing hydrolysis of nucleotide substrates: MazG-type enzymes act on nucleoside (p)ppGpp-type and triphosphate substrates, while HisE-type (phosphoribosyl-ATP pyrophosphatase) enzymes act on phosphoribosyl-ATP in histidine biosynthesis. The two substrates differ, so the shared chemistry does not imply shared substrate specificity or a shared pathway role. The d1y6xa1 label denotes domain 1 of chain A of PDB entry 1y6x, so the conclusion applies to that domain only, not to the whole chain or to every HisE-like protein. The SCOPe evidence supports only a superfamily-level evolutionary relationship. It does not justify concluding that d1vmga_ hydrolyzes PRATP, that d1y6xa1 hydrolyzes (p)ppGpp, that either domain has the other's in vivo function, that catalytic residues or mechanisms transfer exactly, or that the relationship holds across all MazG or HisE members. Confirming any functional transfer would require sequence profile or HMM comparison and active-site motif analysis, structural superposition with an agreed similarity score, biochemical assays of substrate specificity, and genetic or in vivo complementation. Those are external evidence types beyond SCOPe classification.
